newsitem.title: JAPAN: IMF gold auction likely in three years -- Rothschild.
newsitem.headline: IMF gold auction likely in three years -- Rothschild.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund is likely to auction some of its gold within the next three years, as Germany would eventually be obliged to drop its opposition to the idea, Robert Guy, director at N.M. Rothschild, said on Friday.
"After a brief period of reflection and bearing in mind that its views are very much in the minority, it appears to me that German policy could well change," he told the Nikkei Gold Conference.

"I believe that IMF auctions will be held within the next three years. The market itself still appears to believe the sales will take place," he said. "The German stalling tactics have not encouraged any rally in the price."

He said a proposal to sell five million ounces of IMF gold, less than one-quarter the amount sold by Belgium's central bank in recent years, was on its face "an extremely practical and modest proposal".
He expected the sale would be spread out over at least two years and would use the proven, effective auction method used when some IMF gold was sold in the 1970s.

The proposal, aired by British officials several years ago as a means to raise debt-relief funds for poor nations, was shelved at the twice-yearly IMF meeting early this month due to opposition from Germany and a few other member nations.

Guy said Germany's opposition may have stemmed from domestic concerns, such as fears that the sale would encourage Germany's opposition parties to seek Bundesbank gold sales to finance the social budget, or that the German people, already wary of accepting the planned Euro single currency in place of the mark, might become worried about the disposal of their country's own gold reserves.
He warned that Germany's stalling of the IMF gold sale, however, could fuel European wariness towards Germany.

"It's a slightly disturbing saga which unfortunately only serves to encourage those...whose fears about the future of the European Union are concentrated on the power to be exercised by its most powerful economic member, Germany itself."
